method: Carry distances are entered in yards or metres, 3 to 400 yd (3 to 366 m), with at most two decimals, for 2 to 14 clubs drawn from a fixed list of 19 so a name cannot be invented and each club can appear once. Distances are converted to yards with 1 yd = 0.9144 m, sorted longest first with ties keeping the typed order, and each gap is the difference between a club and the next shorter one, so the gaps always add up to the span between the longest and shortest club. A gap above 15 yd (13.716 m) is flagged wide, meaning no club covers that distance; a gap below 8 yd (7.3152 m) is tight, and below 3 yd (2.7432 m) the two clubs are twins. The average gap is the span divided by the number of intervals, which is one fewer than the number of clubs. The ideal carry of the k-th club below the longest is longest minus k times the average, so a set spaced exactly on the average puts every club on its own step; the off-ideal column is the actual carry minus that ideal. Reported values are rounded half away from zero to one decimal in the chosen unit, while the flags are decided on the unrounded yard gaps, so a gap of exactly 15 yd is not wide and one of exactly 8 yd is not tight. Total distance (which adds roll), launch data, dispersion, wind, altitude, club fitting and the loft gaps inside a single wedge are out of scope. Pure local arithmetic with no storage, uploads or network use.

sources.title: Carry distance is the landing point of a shot; total distance adds roll, so only carry can be compared club to club across fairways, winds and launches
Common gapping advice for a full set quotes 10 to 15 yards between successive clubs, with a wider gap meaning a distance that has to be manufactured
1 yard = 0.9144 metres exactly, from the 1959 international yard and pound agreement
R&A and USGA Rules of Golf, Rule 4.1b: a player may carry no more than 14 clubs, which bounds the set this tool accepts
